title: Ahanta: The King Who Came Home

pages.text: In July 2009, an aeroplane from the Netherlands landed in Accra carrying an unusual passenger. A group of chiefs from the Western Region, dressed in the dark red and black cloth of mourning, had travelled to Europe to bring him home. He was their king, Badu Bonsu II of Ahanta, and he had been dead for more than 170 years. For all that time, his head had been kept in a glass jar in a Dutch university. How it came to be there, and how it came back, is a story every Ghanaian should know.

For all that time, his head had been kept in a glass jar in a Dutch university.
How it came to be there, and how it came back, is a story every Ghanaian should know.
pages.alt: Chiefs in dark mourning cloth walking down the steps of an aeroplane, one carrying a covered box.

pages.text: The Ahanta live along the beautiful coast between Sekondi-Takoradi and Axim. Their old capital was Busua. Cape Three Points, the most southerly tip of Ghana, lies in their land. In 1656, the Ahanta chiefs signed a treaty with the Dutch at the town of Butre. In it, they placed themselves under Dutch protection, and the Dutch built a fort on the hill there. For nearly two hundred years, the treaty was kept. The Ahanta governed themselves, and the Dutch traded. Few agreements between Africans and Europeans lasted so long. It is remembered as the Treaty of Butre.

pages.text: By the 1830s, things had changed. The Dutch were behaving less like partners and more like masters. In 1837, they quarrelled with King Badu Bonsu II. Dutch officials tried to call him to account and marched to his town. The king refused to be ordered about in his own land. There was fighting, and two Dutch officials were killed. To the Ahanta, the king was defending his people’s rights. To the Dutch, he was a rebel who had to be made an example of. They sent for soldiers and warships.

pages.text: In 1838, a Dutch force landed. The Ahanta fought, but they were defeated. Badu Bonsu II was captured, put on trial by the Dutch, and hanged. His body was then treated with great disrespect. A doctor removed the head and sent it to the Netherlands, where scientists of that time collected human remains from other parts of the world to study them. The Dutch also ended the Ahanta kingship and ruled the area more directly. Many Ahanta were sent away as prisoners. The people were left without a king and without his body to bury.

pages.text: The jar stayed on a shelf in a medical collection in the Dutch city of Leiden. For many years, nobody outside knew of it. Then a Dutch writer who was researching a book about Ghana learned that it was there. The news reached Ghana, and in 2008 the government asked for the king’s return. The Dutch government agreed and expressed its regret. In 2009, Ahanta chiefs went to the Netherlands. They held a ceremony, poured libation, and received the head of their king. The promise of protection made at Butre had been broken long before. Now, at least, one wrong was put right.

pages.text: Why does this matter today? In our traditions, a person who has not been properly buried is not at rest, and neither are his people. All over the world, museums and universities are now being asked to return human remains and sacred objects that were taken in colonial times. Each return allows people to tell their own history and to mourn in their own way. The Ahanta waited patiently and asked firmly, and they were heard. Dignity can be delayed for a very long time, but it should never be given up.

activities.question: What did the Treaty of Butre do in 1656?
options: It placed the Ahanta under Dutch protection
It sold Ahanta land to the British

activities.question: Why did the quarrel of 1837 begin?
options: The Ahanta attacked a Dutch ship
The Dutch were acting as masters, and the king refused to be ordered about

activities.question: How did Ghana learn where the king’s head was?
options: It was shown on Dutch television every year
A Dutch writer researching a book found out and the news reached Ghana
The Ahanta chiefs had always known

activities.question: Apply it: A museum abroad holds a sacred stool taken from a Ghanaian town in colonial times. Following the Ahanta example, what should the town do?
options: Ask firmly and respectfully, through the proper channels, for its return
Take something from the museum in exchange

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: The Ahanta and the Dutch sign a treaty at Butre
King Badu Bonsu II quarrels with Dutch officials
The king is captured and executed
Ghana asks the Netherlands to return the king’s head
Ahanta chiefs bring their king home
